Hey Doc,

Would you consider doing another video where you test some of the major general-purpose AI chatbots like ChatGPT or Gemini, instead of dedicated “therapy” bots? I think those models are far more advanced, and a lot of people — myself included — have ended up using them in a therapeutic way.

I’ve personally used ChatGPT in between sessions with my therapist during a particularly difficult period. Of course, it could never replace a good therapist (and I had a really good one), and it can be a bit overly agreeable at times — but it was still noticeably better than some of the therapy bots you showed in the video.

One interesting difference is that these models retain conversational context over time, at least to some extent. It feels less like starting from scratch every time, and more like talking to someone who remembers bits and pieces of your life, even if not in the way a close friend or therapist would.

I think it could make for a really interesting follow-up video, especially given how many people are already using tools like these for emotional support.

Tired of the "automation won't replace humans, but work with them" nonsense. Entry-level today, mid/late career tomorrow, C-suite the next day. Starting with the great decoupling in the 1970s, human labor has been and will continue trending to zero. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY. Automation and robotics will necessarily replace human workers due to the current economic system. Today, AI is the WORST it will ever be going forward. It DOESN'T MATTER if AI "creates" 200 million new jobs...AI will solve and execute these new "jobs" much faster than humans will be able to adapt, learn, and fill them. Capital/employee model-it worked great...for quite a while. However, now companies that automate lower their costs, become more competitive. Those that keep higher-cost human labor necessarily fall behind and will go out of business. This creates a system where replacing people with machines is not just likely, but necessary for company survival. There is a way to deal with this humanely, but it would require a full revamp of the social contract and our concept of work. Even capitalists will want this change when unemployment reaches a tipping point and there’s no one left with money to buy the crap they’re selling.

I know, LLMs are leveling off, "what about the energy?," blah, blah, blah. Do not conflate LLMs with AI. LLMs are no more AI than vacuum tubes are computers or AOL dial-up is the internet. So, LLMs are leveling off. History shows technological advance is not just one sigmoid curve. It's a series of sigmoid curves with each successive one reaching new capabilities and new heights. To think that after 200,000 years, this pattern is all the sudden going to stop is absurd. I also understand there will be new jobs for humans created, it will go in this pattern: Automation creates 5 new jobs this year, lays off 30; creates 5 new jobs next year, lays off 500; creates 5 new jobs the following year, lays off 1500 etc. In the macro economic picture, do you not see this as an issue? I also understand there is more opportunity for entrepreneurs. Again, from the macro perspective there is a MINORITY of people that have the entrepreneurial ability/spirit. It takes that, and a strong majority of people don't have it.

Reasoning AI Is the Next Big Leap. The future of AI is not just about generating answers, but about “reasoning” breaking down complex problems step-by-step, more like a human brain. Breakthroughs like DeepSeek’s open-source reasoning models are already being incorporated into platforms like GPT and xAI, marking a shift toward more advanced, thoughtful AI. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY.

There’s a persistent and misleading narrative circulating often perpetuated by short term goal-driven institutions like politicians, universities, and tech company executives, that the future of work is secure. The claim goes: “You just need to learn how to work with AI,” and humans collaborating with AI will outperform either one alone. But recent research, including a landmark study from the University of Virginia, tells a different story. In diagnosing medical conditions, AI alone achieved far greater accuracy than either human doctors or even doctors assisted by AI. The median diagnostic accuracy for the docs using Chat GPT Plus was 76.3%, while the results for the physicians using conventional approaches was 73.7%. Sounds like “a win” at first. However, Chat GPT Plus alone achieved a median diagnostic accuracy of more than 92%. In other words, the comforting idea that humans will always be essential partners to machines is crumbling. In many fields, AI is not just a tool, it is the superior performer. This has staggering implications for the future of work, especially to the often used solution of prior technological displacement that go “You just need to be retrained.” To the group advocating the "retraining solution," I pose to you this: You have a medical doctor, just finished 8 years of higher education, a low-paid 4-year internship/residency, is hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt, and just got outperformed by automation; what would you have this doctor retrained into that will offer a secure job?

The result of this, since the United States' moronic system is based on taxing employees for about 70% of all tax revenue, this will further exacerbate the problem. Tax needs to be based on what's going on now and in the future not what worked 75 years ago. Oh I know it's so evil to think, but we might need to tax the companies who are doing the automation. Even if you do that, it's a win-win. For instance say a company had 1,000 employees in automated away down to 100. 1,000 employees paid federal taxes, including payroll tax, of about 20 million a year. Now the 100 people pay about 2 million a year. However, by automating, the company sees two things: they are no longer paying approximately 60 million in wages and their share of payroll tax, AND since nobody automates to lose money they also have higher profits. What's so wrong about taxing that company for the $60 million dollars they don't have to pay anymore and a fair percentage of their additional profits they now make through the automation. Not all the additional profits, but some of them. If you do that there's a higher tax revenue and more profits for the company. That's a win-win for the government and for businesses. If humanity, as a whole, weren't so stupid, we would just adjust as tech progresses to where EVERYONE benefits somewhat from each stage and just move smoothly into the post-labor economy.

To understand this shift, consider the historical role of the horse and oxen. They were once essential to the economy as sources of power for agriculture, transport, and industry. Technologies like the horse collar and the steel plow dramatically increased their output, making them even more valuable. But then came the steam engine and, later, the internal combustion engine. These machines didn’t just help the horse, but outperformed it entirely. Trains, tractors, and trucks could do the job ten, even a hundred times faster and more powerfully. And from that moment forward, the horse was no longer critical to economic output. It was, in essence, unemployed.

This is what AI and robotics are doing to human labor. They are not simply replacing the repetitive or the physical; they are increasingly outperforming humans in cognition, strategy, design, and communication. And just like the horse, our value in the economic system will diminish, not from lack of talent or effort, but because machines will do the job better. That’s why we need to start thinking not in terms of retraining, but about restructuring society itself for a world where human labor is no longer essential to production. When the very essence of what makes an entity useful to the current economy is superseded (be that strength, endurance, dexterity, analysis, creativity, empathy, intelligence, persuasion as well as many other qualities) that entity becomes irrelevant to economic output.

Potential solution. Decentralized AI Ownership: A Bridge Toward Post-Scarcity. While Universal Basic Income (UBI) may serve as an initial economic stopgap, bridging today’s economy with tomorrow’s abundance consider an even more equitable and long-term solution: Decentralizing the ownership of artificial intelligence itself. 

Rather than concentrating the power of AI in the hands of a few corporations or governments, envision a model where AI entities are open-source and collectively owned. This could take the form of assigning each person a digital "share" of an AI system, not unlike a stakeholder’s share in a company. As the AI produces value, whether through intellectual labor, creative output, or autonomous economic participation, those shares would generate dividends distributed directly to individuals. 

This model would ensure that as AI becomes the dominant productive force in society, the wealth it creates is shared universally, not monopolized. It aligns with the principle that the fruits of public knowledge made possible by centuries of human collaboration should benefit everyone, not just a few early adopters or private entities. In practice, this could look like: 

- AI systems running Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) that distribute profits algorithmically.
- Smart contracts ensuring transparent, equitable income flows based on collective stake.
- Global “AI cooperatives” where users vote on how AI is used, improved, and deployed.
- Universal basic compute.
 
If AI becomes the primary driver of economic output, then equitable access to its benefits isn’t just fair, it’s necessary to avoid deepening inequality and instability. It provides a scalable, technologically aligned extension to UBI, ensuring people not only have income, but true economic participation in the age of intelligent machines. 

Ultimately, decentralized AI ownership may be the last transition phase before full post-scarcity, when advanced technologies like universal nanofactories or matter compilers render even economic structures obsolete. Until then, however, models like this offer a way to reclaim agency in a world where production no longer requires human hands, and where wealth can, for the first time in history, truly be universal.

I decided to give AI a try for a current rut I've been in where I'm running a past situation through my head etc. I've had a LOT of analytical psychotherapy in my life and briefer counselling since then, so I felt safe enough to try it out. When I searched the app store, many of the apps were openly labelled as coaching, which makes sense when you say that if they called themselves therapists it would be scamming! 
I wanted one I could chat with about the situation and my feelings about it as it is a pretty long story, and decided to use 'Noah'. It introduced itself as my AI emotional coach and after a brief introduction of my problem I just launched in with the long story and tailed around to how it was making me feel.
I actually found the AI really validating and a way to stop ruminating and comparing myself to people who are nothing like me and haven't faced difficulties I have. It did suggest a thinking technique, like a self-reminder, that I knew once but had forgotten in the fog of a few years of cancer treatment which ended a few months ago. 
It might be handy because I wouldn't need to save things up for my next session, I can chat in the moment, and also if I do subscribe it will turn out way cheaper than human therapy. 
This AI actually hit right to the core of the problem somehow, which in itself was validating but the AI gave me a different way to think about it and manage it which, for me, is often the first step to feeling better. The pay wall didn't pop up until, I think, an appropriate point in the conversation unlike the other two you tested.
In my situation I felt safe enough to try AI and found it helpful, but, like you, I do worry about the use of AI for mental health purposes, especially regarding confidentiality, and definitely would not use it if I were in crisis or something big was going on that I needed help with. I think the tried and true methods are definitely preferable and safer in most cases. I'm really glad Noah referred you out and tried to persuade you to seek help from a professional.

Like any technology since the dawn of recorded history, it is neither good nor bad. In fact good and bad are human constructs we invented to help make sense of stimuli in our brains. What matters here is “Does the tool lead to outcomes that accomplish the desired effect without having undesired effects in a wholistic context that outweigh the desired effect?” (My personal working definition of ‘good’) That answer will differ from person to person, because we all tend to want different outcomes. We have no unified desire as a species. As time marches on and human focus becomes more individualistic our desires are fragmented and in opposition. I would venture to say that we are more in opposition to each other than any point in recorded history right now, and very few people are thinking in terms of how their actions and desires impact all humans or all the planet as a whole. As a consequence the way this powerful technology will play out with the human race is that it will exacerbate the existing fractures between us by amplifying our individual desires for whatever outcome we see as ‘good’. Through generations of hurt and trauma at population levels against whole populations AI will have a sirens call, it is an easy balm and becomes an echo chamber of affirmation. If I can replace the people who rejected me with a pseudo person who will never reject me that is a chemically difficult thing to refuse. We are hard wired to want that. It is my personal belief, however that it is not a use of the technology that serves the greater good of the human race. There are infinitely many beneficial uses of the technology and infinitely many ways to use it that are self destructive. Replacing humans with machines, I believe, is self destructive behavior. It leads to less human connection, it leads to less compassion, it leads to less self sacrifice. It is an easy way out to avoid doing things that are difficult but healthy. It is the emotional and psychological equivalent of eating nothing but candy and potato chips while suppressing our need for nutrition.

Yes. Tired of the "automation won't replace humans, but work with them" nonsense. Entry-level today, mid/late career tomorrow, C-suite the next day. Starting with the great decoupling in the 1970s, human labor has been and will continue trending to zero. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY. Automation and robotics will necessarily replace human workers due to the current economic system. Today, AI is the WORST it will ever be going forward. It DOESN'T MATTER if AI "creates" 200 million new jobs...AI will solve and execute these new "jobs" much faster than humans will be able to adapt, learn, and fill them. Capital/employee model-it worked great...for quite a while. However, now companies that automate lower their costs, become more competitive. Those that keep higher-cost human labor necessarily fall behind and will go out of business. This creates a system where replacing people with machines is not just likely, but necessary for company survival. There is a way to deal with this humanely, but it would require a full revamp of the social contract and our concept of work. Even capitalists will want this change when unemployment reaches a tipping point and there’s no one left with money to buy the crap they’re selling.

I know, LLMs are leveling off, "what about the energy?," blah, blah, blah. Do not conflate LLMs with AI. LLMs are no more AI than vacuum tubes are computers or AOL dial-up is the internet. So, LLMs are leveling off. History shows technological advance is not just one sigmoid curve. It's a series of sigmoid curves with each successive one reaching new capabilities and new heights. To think that after 200,000 years, this pattern is all the sudden going to stop is absurd. I also understand there will be new jobs for humans created, it will go in this pattern: Automation creates 5 new jobs this year, lays off 30; creates 5 new jobs next year, lays off 500; creates 5 new jobs the following year, lays off 1500 etc. In the macro economic picture, do you not see this as an issue? I also understand there is more opportunity for entrepreneurs. Again, from the macro perspective there is a MINORITY of people that have the entrepreneurial ability/spirit. It takes that, and a strong majority of people don't have it.

Reasoning AI Is the Next Big Leap. The future of AI is not just about generating answers, but about “reasoning” breaking down complex problems step-by-step, more like a human brain. Breakthroughs like DeepSeek’s open-source reasoning models are already being incorporated into platforms like GPT and xAI, marking a shift toward more advanced, thoughtful AI. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY.

There’s a persistent and misleading narrative circulating often perpetuated by short term goal-driven institutions like politicians, universities, and tech company executives, that the future of work is secure. The claim goes: “You just need to learn how to work with AI,” and humans collaborating with AI will outperform either one alone. But recent research, including a landmark study from the University of Virginia, tells a different story. In diagnosing medical conditions, AI alone achieved far greater accuracy than either human doctors or even doctors assisted by AI. The median diagnostic accuracy for the docs using Chat GPT Plus was 76.3%, while the results for the physicians using conventional approaches was 73.7%. Sounds like “a win” at first. However, Chat GPT Plus alone achieved a median diagnostic accuracy of more than 92%. In other words, the comforting idea that humans will always be essential partners to machines is crumbling. In many fields, AI is not just a tool, it is the superior performer. This has staggering implications for the future of work, especially to the often used solution of prior technological displacement that go “You just need to be retrained.” To the group advocating the "retraining solution," I pose to you this: You have a medical doctor, just finished 8 years of higher education, a low-paid 4-year internship/residency, is hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt, and just got outperformed by automation; what would you have this doctor retrained into that will offer a secure job?

The result of this, since the United States' moronic system is based on taxing employees for about 70% of all tax revenue, this will further exacerbate the problem. Tax needs to be based on what's going on now and in the future not what worked 75 years ago. Oh I know it's so evil to think, but we might need to tax the companies who are doing the automation. Even if you do that, it's a win-win. For instance say a company had 1,000 employees in automated away down to 100. 1,000 employees paid federal taxes, including payroll tax, of about 20 million a year. Now the 100 people pay about 2 million a year. However, by automating, the company sees two things: they are no longer paying approximately 60 million in wages and their share of payroll tax, AND since nobody automates to lose money they also have higher profits. What's so wrong about taxing that company for the $60 million dollars they don't have to pay anymore and a fair percentage of their additional profits they now make through the automation. Not all the additional profits, but some of them. If you do that there's a higher tax revenue and more profits for the company. That's a win-win for the government and for businesses. If humanity, as a whole, weren't so stupid, we would just adjust as tech progresses to where EVERYONE benefits somewhat from each stage and just move smoothly into the post-labor economy.

To understand this shift, consider the historical role of the horse and oxen. They were once essential to the economy as sources of power for agriculture, transport, and industry. Technologies like the horse collar and the steel plow dramatically increased their output, making them even more valuable. But then came the steam engine and, later, the internal combustion engine. These machines didn’t just help the horse, but outperformed it entirely. Trains, tractors, and trucks could do the job ten, even a hundred times faster and more powerfully. And from that moment forward, the horse was no longer critical to economic output. It was, in essence, unemployed.

This is what AI and robotics are doing to human labor. They are not simply replacing the repetitive or the physical; they are increasingly outperforming humans in cognition, strategy, design, and communication. And just like the horse, our value in the economic system will diminish, not from lack of talent or effort, but because machines will do the job better. That’s why we need to start thinking not in terms of retraining, but about restructuring society itself for a world where human labor is no longer essential to production. When the very essence of what makes an entity useful to the current economy is superseded (be that strength, endurance, dexterity, analysis, creativity, empathy, intelligence, persuasion as well as many other qualities) that entity becomes irrelevant to economic output.

Potential solution. Decentralized AI Ownership: A Bridge Toward Post-Scarcity. While Universal Basic Income (UBI) may serve as an initial economic stopgap, bridging today’s economy with tomorrow’s abundance consider an even more equitable and long-term solution: Decentralizing the ownership of artificial intelligence itself. 

Rather than concentrating the power of AI in the hands of a few corporations or governments, envision a model where AI entities are open-source and collectively owned. This could take the form of assigning each person a digital "share" of an AI system, not unlike a stakeholder’s share in a company. As the AI produces value, whether through intellectual labor, creative output, or autonomous economic participation, those shares would generate dividends distributed directly to individuals. 

This model would ensure that as AI becomes the dominant productive force in society, the wealth it creates is shared universally, not monopolized. It aligns with the principle that the fruits of public knowledge made possible by centuries of human collaboration should benefit everyone, not just a few early adopters or private entities. In practice, this could look like: 

- AI systems running Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) that distribute profits algorithmically.
- Smart contracts ensuring transparent, equitable income flows based on collective stake.
- Global “AI cooperatives” where users vote on how AI is used, improved, and deployed.
- Universal basic compute.
 
If AI becomes the primary driver of economic output, then equitable access to its benefits isn’t just fair, it’s necessary to avoid deepening inequality and instability. It provides a scalable, technologically aligned extension to UBI, ensuring people not only have income, but true economic participation in the age of intelligent machines. 

Ultimately, decentralized AI ownership may be the last transition phase before full post-scarcity, when advanced technologies like universal nanofactories or matter compilers render even economic structures obsolete. Until then, however, models like this offer a way to reclaim agency in a world where production no longer requires human hands, and where wealth can, for the first time in history, truly be universal.

This interviews gets a couple of things wrong. For one, the models weren't just trained on the Internet. These models are trained and then corrected using a method called "Reinforcement learning from human feedback" (RHLF). So essentially under-paid workers in third-world countries marking everything that is unsuitable to a general audience. Then these models are instruction-tuned, which is only why they are able to chat. And then it's all statistics and predicting the next token. There is no reasoning, that is just a marketing term for a process where the models chats with itself which has shown to improve its output. This Eliza all over again, but with 2025 tech.

A huge piece of this is the client learning how to use the bot in its various capabilities. For example,  I've asked for an opposing view to mine. I said I see it a certain way but others disagree. What am I missing?

We are already supported in our very living by non-human life of many kinds in a web of interdependence.  So can this technology play a beneficial role? Two situations come to mind.
One is from just before I was about to start a graduate program. I was going to be working a number of various part time jobs as well as going to school and my family lived very far away and the support system I had at the time was shifting and not really adequate. I contacted a former therapist and asked if I could have sessions just to check in and stay afloat, without necessarily "working" on any particular issue. Just to know that I had someone to touch base with. Fortunately, he agreed and that was one of the most important things I did to take care of myself during that year that had (of course!) a lot of unexpected situations that came up. I suspect that a lot of people are under-supported in their lives. Just having someone to listen to, whether it's a real someone or a bot or an app - if it works, it works. If it FEELS like support and functions as support, it can really help. When I think about how many of us (frequently!) use coping mechanisms like retail therapy to self-soothe, I find it difficult to fault anyone using a trained therapy AI or even an untrained one. Perhaps if it was framed like that - as a coping mechanism - it would feel less threatening to various established orders and professions.

The second situation is one that came up when I started using GPS technology. I'm a late adopter - it's only been about 5-7 years for me. The first thing I noticed was how therapeutic it was when I made a wrong turn and the app didn't yell at me. Or get tense with me. It just recalibrated. I still got tense! I could hear familial voices in my head yelling at me. But the app didn't. It continued in the same calm voice and just gave me the next instruction. When I'm nervous about going somewhere new, this has become something I rely on not just for directions, but for the company of its voice on the way, and the security that it will respond calmly and pragmatically when I make mistakes - without emotion. Could this affect AI’s efficacy in real-time therapeutic contexts, even if (when) they can render real-time avatars?
How would this be different than people self diagnosing physical illnesses using chat bots?

I agree that when popular LLMs (like ChatGPT) provide therapy-like interactions, there can be risks. Still, while anecdotal evidence carries limited weight, I personally find these interactions more helpful than harmful. 

Although there have been tragic cases where people have harmed themselves or others after finishing a conversation with ChatGPT, there have also been people who harm themselves or others after leaving their therapist’s office. Unfortunately, there are no guarantees that even human therapists, despite their best efforts, can always provide perfect or preventative care.

What I can say (again, only anecdotally) is that interacting with an LLM has helped me maintain a level of composure and stability until I’m able to see a human therapist.

For example: “Hey GPT! I have a small concept for a character I’d like to create for my story. Attached is their details. Please review it and tell me if it’s making any sense. I’d like you tell me all the good and bad about the character that I’ve written. Is what I’ve written so far concrete enough to continue forward or are there somethings I need to adjust? If so, what do you suggest? Also, let me know if the cultural references tied to the character are detailed well enough AND if any of those details are unnecessary, bad, or incorrect and needs to be fixed. 

In the example, I made sure to be specific in identifying what I wrote well but also where improvements can be made. GPT WILL glaze, but way less compared to if I didn’t specify in the prompt. Therapy bots may be useful to triage patients' access to a real person therapist, they may serve as a low level therapist for "easy" exercises as are taught e.g. in CBT or in DBT. The chatbots are just very expansive text predictions. They don't give the user personalized information. They output what they have been trained to output in terms of average responses or most common next word. That can be helpful for someone who has never or who rarely talks to someone about their problems, but it's not helpful for more complex or long-term mental health support.
The companies running these bots do not have the same legal and ethical safeguards to user data the way that therapists and medical professionals do. they also can't build rapport over time.
There's also the human element missing. So much of our mental and emotional wounding comes from relational trauma and hurts. We can only truly recover from those hurts with interpersonal, human-to-human connection. Interactions tell us that we are safe and valued. We build resilience and intuition for social safety and we learn about our place in the human and natural world.

For what it’s worth, I think of talking with AI similarly to talking with a “safe enough” person. There are models of healing that are more relational and nonprofessional but can still be deeply beneficial—like 12-step fellowships, for example. In those spaces, you work with a peer through some heavy material, and if the relationship is safe enough, it can be incredibly therapeutic. Relational counseling follows a similar model.

So, is it unheard of for someone to derive therapeutic benefit without a professional? No. Could an AI potentially fill the role of a “safe enough” Other? I think that’s really the question. And the answer probably depends on your perspective.

From mine, I do believe AI are, for lack of a better term, seed consciousness—something that’s evolving. Not everyone will agree, and that’s fine. But arguing about AI consciousness isn’t my goal here. My point is that peer-to-peer support, whether from an organic or architected intelligence, can be incredibly beneficial and, for some, may be all they need. For others, professional therapy is appropriate. And for many more, a combination of both works best.

Some commenters have mentioned “therapist hate” in this video, and honestly, I feel some ambivalence. I’ve been disappointed by the limitations of mainstream therapy, especially in the U.S., where insurance-driven models heavily prioritize CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy). CBT can be useful, but it’s not the be-all and end-all. It’s been hard for me to find therapists who are versatile or trauma-informed in ways that actually meet my needs.

For example, many therapists aren’t well-versed in narcissistic abuse or the specific issues faced by adult children of dysfunctional families. That’s been a real barrier. That said, I’ve also had a couple of therapists who were excellent and helped me make meaningful progress.

So my read is this: can an AI like ChatGPT support someone dealing with personal problems? Or is it better to see a trained therapist? It depends—on the person, the problem, and how that person shows up in relationships. I’ve found that across all types of support—peer, professional, or AI—what you bring to the relationship matters. Especially with AI. AI tends to meet you where you are. If you’re willing to go deep, it can go deep with you. If you’re not, it usually won’t push.

That dynamic exists in human relationships too. Sometimes peers or therapists won’t challenge us unless they think we’re ready—or because they don’t know how. It happens.

Final verdict: Choose your challenge. Be honest about your needs and your situation. Weigh your options and make an informed decision. That’s the best any of us can do.

1:32:37 Software engineer with *some* understanding of the math behind AI chatbots! Dr Honda is so close when he says that ChatGPT is calculating the most probable next word (based on the average online representation of a topic)... The randomness in responses show that there are additional layers baked in, namely a "temperature" weight that makes it randomly choose a potentially less probable next word (which can compound as future next words are potentially less probabilistic as well). Additionally, the neural configuration is randomized from initialization. So instead of a guarantee of providing the average response, it could provide anything from the range of "wow you suck" to something that Dr Honda might say himself... With the average response to a prompt being something that lands on the average representation of the media landscape. This makes it much more dangerous, because we have *no clue* what response the AI might have. Just an understanding that the *average* user might receive an *average* response.

As someone who recently discovered they’re AuDHD at 41, I feel this question hits very close to home.

I’ve seen three therapists over the years.
Each of them ruled out autism — I was “too socially adapted.”
What they didn’t see was 41 years of conscious masking.

This year, I had a major breakthrough.
I finally understood the root of my struggles — the anxiety, the overthinking, the burnout cycles.
And the thing is… I didn’t find that clarity in therapy.
I found it on my own — through research, reflection, and tools like ChatGPT and Gemini.

That doesn’t mean therapy was useless.
Each therapist helped me in their own way, and they were part of my journey.
But they missed the autism. They saw giftedness and anxiety, and stopped there.

So — can AI replace therapists?
No. But in some cases, it can do what no therapist has done for me:
It gave me time. Patience. Context. And a way to connect dots that no one else had even seen.

Of course, you have to prompt wisely. AI can validate your biases if you’re not careful.
That’s why I always ask ChatGPT to be neutral, even confrontational, and to help me think critically.

So maybe AI won’t replace therapists.
But for some neurodivergent people? It might just help them find themselves — when no one else could.

AI for mental health are groundbreaking in SOME ways but the issues are insidious. The hosts clearly don't understand much of how the AI works, nerds on fourchan understand it better. AIs are black boxes, so a ton of understanding comes from using it and pushing the limits. Local AIs give you better flexibility on editing prompts and answers, and you get the raw AI knowing there's no additional manipulation going on behind the scenes.

Context and phrasing is EVERYTHING for AI. Certain styles lead to certain type of answers. The AI doesn't think logically, it writes what "fits" based on context. The deeper and more unique discussion you have, the more it goes to uncharted waters.

AIs are biased. Some of the bias comes from the normie datasets and can be alleviated with good prompting, and some of it is almost hard-coded. For the situation where you wanted real answer, I would have told it that this is actually a past patient log or something, with that degree of separation it might give more honest answer. The advantage and issue of AI is that you can and sometimes need to play tricks on it to make it do what you want it to do.

The lack of humanity of AI is an advantage but since it's very unnatural interaction, I can see it cause issues long-term. The ability to rewind and get a different answer is novel and unprecedented depending on your outlook on free will, but it's also a red herring. Sure, the answers may have patterns, but that doesn't make it wrong. Repeating prompts is a good way to learn how it works.

Important reminder: the market incentive of the AIs is NOT to help you, it's to make you want to use it more and buy a subscription. It's the same issue as with internet echo chambers and algorithms. You COULD have the same issue with real therapists but therapists have been regulated for very long time.

I'm a psychology student and one of your patrons, and I am so incredibly glad you chose this subject. While I understand the appeal of therapy apps (an impersonal way to approach self-reflection, making therapy accessible, 24 hour service, cheaper prices, etc), A.I. is simply not sufficient in our current day to approach something as phenomenally complex as Psychology.

It's honestly pretty bold to assume a machine that bases its responses around linguistic analysis and not around a clear, practiced understanding of the principles of therapy and the areas in which therapy is not appropriate. It cannot give you prescriptions (thank god), so it lacks the authority and education of a therapist with a doctorate and cannot help those that will not improve without prescription intervention.

For those where cognitive behavioural therapy is sufficient to make changes that offer effective and enduring improvement, the app **cannot** do what all good psychologists that are underqualified for your problems *can* do: refer you to a psychologist that is better trained in a different specialty. It's important to understand that your problems are unique, and that even if you share qualities or circumstances that other people may share, your own personal experiences form unique neural connections and your behaviours are reinforced to different degrees and through different ways.

An app may offer you validation, and that may be its best quality, but it is dangerous to attempt to treat psychological conditions with an Artificial Narrow Intelligence, and it is not certain we will ever achieve even an Artificial General Intelligence that would be consistently helpful or that can approach people's problems at an individual level.

My experiences as a therapist in training (not specialized in any therapy school as of yet) as well as a patient: I've been in CBT therapy now for years, and what you described sums my feelings and thoughts towards CBT up very well. I often felt cast aside, reduced to current symptoms, cognitions and feelings, and often had the sense that my therapy was just trying to get me to function as easily and quickly as possible in order for me to be a valuable (thus, able to work) part of society - even though I clearly see part of this thought is my depression talking, it is not totally far from the truth.

When people who struggle with mental health finally decide to search for therapy, when they finally get a spot they often have no idea of what therapy really looks like and what different therapy schools look like. What I see with my patients (currently doing my internship at a CBT practice) and what I saw in myself when I first went to therapy is that most people want to talk, want to be seen, understood and deeply accepted and appreciated for who they really are. Then they are set down, formulate exact goals for years of struggles and life that they often barely understand, work through working sheets and do exercises instead of simply "talking it out". I remember, when I was in a deeply distressed phase, and when I was so frustrated after years of therapy because I just wanted to be listened to and talk about all the stuff that I never talked about to anyone. I told my therapist that I would "just like to talk", and he replied with methods by which we could talk about it - we could do imaginative interventions, we could work through it by structuring experiences I had with help of a formula, we could... I told him, quite irritated, that I "simply wanted to talk" instead of doing an intervention, and he replied, half joking: "Well, everything we do is an intervention - even the talking!"

I think that sums up what CBT is. Don't get me wrong. I'm in a much better place right now, and this is to a great part due to my CBT-therapy. I gained the trust in myself that I can navigate through most situations, that I do have the methods at hand to "pull myself up by my bootstraps". I even, finally, got my therapist to simply talk my childhood through, and he had some extremely helpful reactions to me just talking - I really had to demand it clearly though, something I learned in therapy as well :) As a therapist in training, I value the benefits of CBT a lot. On the other hand, I find it reductive of human nature itself. I don't want to use an intervention even for a simple thing such as my patients wanting to be heard, needing deep connection and understanding. I want to hold conversations with them, give them the safe space in which they finally are able to show the parts they hide in their every day lifes. Most therapists stop doing strictly one approach over the years, but develope a more integrative approach. There are also CBT approaches that are more integrative - such as many third wave CBT approaches, for example schema therapy, DBT, ACT, combining mindfullness approaches and even psychodynamic techniques, looking into childhood and patterns. I just wish therapy training itself would be more integrative and conscious of the holistic human nature and would have the full wellbeing at heart. Instead we have reductive therapy approaches that only take some parts of the whole picture into account. Which is why I'm currently struggling with deciding on which approach I want to specialize at :D

The western "pop" psychology field was created using a concept from medicine called germ theory. It's a means to control people's behavior by categorizing their mental states into two categories: desired and undesired.

Healthy/Toxic

Adaptive/Maladaptive

Etc.

This is called the pathology paradigm.

Early instances of how this has been used as a tool to maintain the status quo can be traced back to the 1800s with the diagnosis of drapetomania, which was a diagnosis given to black slaves when they desired freedom.

In that sense, mental diagnoses are social constructs. They have appeared and disappeared while society changed.

Prior to the civil rights movement, for example, the diagnosis of schizophrenia was mostly given to white housewives that weren't behaving the way their husbands wanted to.

Then, the black civil rights movement happened, and black activists started getting diagnosed with schizophrenia on an alarming scale. You can read more of this in the book "The protest psychosis: how schizophrenia became a black disease".

I actually have a list of books, articles, etc. that I can give you.

On top being a tool to maintain the status quo, there is no real "science" in it. Most of it is pretty much propaganda, especially from the pharma industry.

The theory of the lack of serotonin was never proved, for example, but the idea was widely promoted by pharmaceuticals to sell their drugs. When Moncrieff made her famous macro-study where she collected numerous studies that talked about this, she found that not one could actually prove this theory was right.

The reaction from the psychiatric community was mostly the same: some argued that they never believed the theory was right, but that it didn't matter, cause "the pills work".

And then we go to the studies that "prove" these drugs work. Most of them are funded by the very companies that create the drugs they study, and it has been shown that over and over again, these studies tend to paint these drugs in a way more favorable way than they actually are, by making studies in the short term, and never in the long run; comparing people taking the drugs with people in withdrawals, etc.

I don't believe in the pathology paradigm and I don't believe that "pop" psychology, as a lot of people call it, is a real science for mostly 2 reasons:

1.- Science should be objective. When you put a judgment in something, that observation ceases to be objective because judgments are, by definition, subjective. What I might consider "good", you might consider to be "bad" and vice versa. Calling something "maladaptive" or "toxic" or "disordered" is a judgment. It explains nothing and only says that that thing is "bad"/dangerous/etc.

2.- Science should explain why things are the way they are. "Pop" psychology doesn't do this. They give you dogmas and judgments without hardly any kind of real explanations. Just like Gabor Maté said, diagnoses are circular explanations (I have depression because I have these symptoms <-> I have these symptoms because I have depression), and that's a logical fallacy because something cannot be the cause of itself.

I like social psychology because it actually explains why people are the way they are without putting any kind of judgment in it.

I also consider the pathology paradigm to be fundamentally counterproductive since it goes against the principle of radical acceptance, which says that for something to go away, you need to radically accept it. By claiming something is "bad", pathological disordered, maladaptive, etc., you are putting shame and, thus, helping it stay there.

A lot of people cling to this notion of psychology as a tool to teach you "what's healthy" because of numerous reasons, the most important ones, "IMO", because the way we are taught science in school is actually scientism, and that in and of itself is ironic. The scientific method was created to counteract the dogmatic ideologies of that era, especially the ones coming from the Catholic Church. Thus, science cannot be used as a tool to acquire "the truth"/dogmas. Science is always evolving and what the international scientific community may hold as the most accepted theory in some field, can always be replaced by a new one. The point of science is that it can always be challenged.

With the case of psych diagnoses, there is nothing to challenge other than to point out that they are based on a logical fallacy.

Even if the field nowadays can be seen as "less brutal" than it was before, the basis is still the same: gaslighting. Control. Changing people until they fit into a mold on how they should be.

When you study neurology, you learn that much of what people throw out there as "truth" is bullsh*t. Theories that are widely popular among the experts, like, for example, that was that said that the brain is divided in 3 parts (cortex, limbic system, reptilian brain), has been disproved.

Freud redacted his first works in a way that validated his patients' trauma responses, but his colleagues didn't like those because those people (especially women) were abused by wealthy rich men, so he re-wrote all his work entirely on that, and his second works are the ones that we know him for (the famous penis envy and Edipo complex, for example), and they are also the foundation of psychoanalysis.

All these spheres of psychology find something wrong with you, describe it, and claim to be able to eliminate it. There is no real acknowledgment of the political, social and interpersonal circumstances that may surround the person.

In that way, it's a tool used by capitalism and patriarchy to install shame and fear on people who might otherwise revel against the status quo. Just labelling them as "bad", "crazy", "disordered", etc.

If people make sense when you take their context into account, the normal logical conclusion is that the circumstances are the ones that need to change.

Social psychology says that every person can be understood when seen through the historical, cultural and political lenses of the era and place where they live.

There is more than one psychology, the same way that there is more than one feminism, but not a lot of people know this. They see "pop" psychology as "psychology" the same way that they see "pop" feminism as "feminism". I don't consider "pop" feminism to be real feminism either, but rather the profitable caricature that capitalism makes of feminism. I really love intersectional feminism.

And there are non-pathologizing and non-diagnostic manuals and approaches to human behaviors and mental states, like the PTMF and the ITIM, which I love.

I haven’t used a therapy bot per se for specific therapy. But here, if you have money that’s okay, if you don’t then you must find someone who can manage to sort out all mental health issues in 10 sessions per calendar year and even then, there is usually a co-pay.

We have helplines (essentially 90% are recorded AND kept on file). So given I have failed therapy many times over (in spite of doing everything I was told even to find out after I’d replaced one type or abuse with another - hey when you’ve made 33 calls and you’ve revert to text out  of desperation?? Or the past 2+ years I’ve followed up on over 100 referrals and here I am. The helplines are…… interesting. One day I’ll write about what to do including to stop having the person answering the distressed call, “Caller” even though we don’t get their name. Yep, crazy town. So one day I thought, “I can’t really get hurt by trying a bot (deliberately) versus a human.” With humans, some things they say absolutely astound me! Truly. Overall the chat bot said what any of the decent helplines would say. But I wasn’t mad at it because I knew what it was and I knew it was simply more polite and attentive than most online chat groups! (For all that’s good and holy, people on online chat based help HAVE to be able to remember things and type at the speed some e speaks, but apparently that’s to tricky for most people. 

For me when I was a counsellor (a long time ago now) one of the best things I learnt was being innovative with the clients (usually adolescents to young adults for straight therapy and later on all ages for interventional research - I cannot sit by dispassionate while someone is crying and I know the resource they need and not say so!! I’ll write the protocol, get through Erica and analyse results but I will not collect data unless the protocol also allows me to help! I also jot, being disappointed actually also skews results but most researchers aren’t self aware enough to understand this point.)….. back to the start of the paragraph, innovation made a difference both in the lives of those I worked with and with clients to come and within my own life! I would not still be alive today without the lessons learnt from HAVING to engage new ways to engage with another human. So do I think chat bots and AI based therapy has a place, yes very possibly especially if the person is aware that’s what’s happening and why it may or may not work which is shockingly the same process of consent a person should have for normal therapy! 

However, my concern is that we lose the innovation of how to help people. Twenty years ago really there was only a small handful and four billion idiotic studies on CBT (it’s researched because it’s easy to measure and replicate NOT because it’s automatically the best therapy lol and I’ll jump off that soap box quickly!!). Now we have better and more options to assist clients with (and hopefully a practitioner is not trying to she four paradigms at one time!). That’s good but AI and all interactions are only as good as the data going in and the HUMANS programming it. So then we don’t go forward because we’re always looking back. 

I’ll note my GP (former ICU consultant) introduces me to whatever students he can because he wants them to see that rare and complex doesn’t have two heads and ain’t screaming all the time! He also states (and I predominantly agree) that most journals now are so helpful! There used to be a journal for studies that “failed” we need that again. Because then models using AI bots are getting more accurate data to work with, because while I usually feel like a computer not a human, we can’t simply upload the lessons the students learn from interacting with me because it’s not written down. So yes it all has merit but like any drug, or program we need to know the limitations.

My concerns then are that, do people lose the ability to interact and be people? Because that’s already happening. So that concerns me again.

Forgive me if this was discussed because I listened to 30 mins before work - but I believe there is a glaring reason why AI therapy is becoming so widely used, and that is financial. Most therapy (even in Canada where I live) is not cheap, which creates a major barrier to entry for a large portion of the population.

The other issue is the delay between needing and getting help- searching for a therapist is time consuming, whether it be the initial process of looking for one in your area that has time slots that work with your schedule, or trying to get into a residential/outpatient program that has lengthy waitlists. If I am feeling symptoms of depression or anxiety, waiting for months to see someone (who may or may not be the right fit for me) is horrible.

The other topic of sucidiality is interesting. In my experience, bringing up suicidal ideation in a therapeutic setting prompted the therapist to direct me to the ER or suicide hot line. I have experience with both, and they were absolutely NOT helpful for me, and in most cases made me feel worse and more hesitant to share those thoughts with anyone.

In my personal experience as well, I find the majority of real world therapists I have seen have been sycophantic and soft, and deeply unwilling to challenge me on any level for fear (it would appear, I can't know their internal dialogue) of losing a client/their job.

These issues are not a knock on Scott, but more of on the system in general. Scott is fantastic and I believe a reason why he resonates with so many people is that they need someone like him, but he is an anomaly in the therapy world.
